parole.significato: Rhinebarge, a single-masted flat-bottomed barge used on the Rhine for wine transportation.
aam, an old Dutch and German unit of measure for liquids.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch abrikoos. Further from Latin praecox.
Borrowed from Dutch overal. Attested since the early 19th century.
From Dutch ansjovis (attested as анчовес in 1724), from Spanish anchoa, from Ligurian anciôa, from Vulgar Latin *apiuva, from Latin aphyē (“small fry”), from Ancient Greek ἀφύη (aphúē).
Borrowed from Dutch appelsien, calqued from French pomme de Sine (“Chinese apple”). For semantic parallels compare пе́рсик (pérsik).
Per Vasmer, probably borrowed from Dutch baai, from French baie (“woolen matter”), from bai (“chestnut-colored, bay”), from Latin badius (“chestnut-colored, bay”). First attested in 1720.
Borrowed from Dutch bakboord or German Backbord.

parole.significato: buoy, a moored float, sea mark, beacon
ballast (heavy material placed in the hold of a vessel)
seizing (means of tying together two thin wires or cables)

parole.testo: From Dutch beurs, possibly via German Börse. First attested in 1717, with an early masculine variant of биржъ in 1705. Further from Latin bursa, from Ancient Greek βύρσα (búrsa).
First attested in 1688 in the nautical sense. Borrowed from Dutch boord or German Bord. Further from Proto-Germanic *burdą.

parole.significato: a type of small, single-masted sailing vessel or small motor vessel; boat

parole.testo: From the earlier form презенинг (prezening), from Dutch presenning.

Borrowed from Dutch broek. First attested in the eighteenth century, but became more popular a hundred years later. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *brōks, whence also English breeches, whence a doublet бри́джи (brídži). Further from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreg- (whence also English break, Latin frang
Borrowed from Dutch beugel or German Bügel.

parole.significato: to tow, to tug (to pull something behind one using a line or chain)
parole.testo: First attested in 1712. Borrowed from Dutch boegseren, from Portuguese puxar, from Latin pulsāre. By surface analysis, букси́р (buksír) + -овать (-ovatʹ) or -и́ровать (-írovatʹ). Unrelated to Russian бу́кса (búksa). The relation with буксова́ть (buksovátʹ) is uncertain.
Borrowed from a Germanic language, probably Dutch boor (“drill”).

According to Chernykh, from Dutch waaier in the early 18th century (revocalized under the influence of веять (vejatʹ)), from waaien (“to blow”), from Middle Dutch wâyen, from Old Dutch *wāien, from Proto-West Germanic *wāan, from Proto-Germanic *wēaną, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (which is als
Borrowed from Dutch haven or Middle Low German haven.

parole.significato: iron hook used for lifting equipment
jack (device for raising and supporting a heavy object)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch dommekracht. For the first part of the word doublet of дюйм (djujm).
Borrowed from Dutch drijven or one of its forms.
Borrowed from Dutch duim, cognate with English thumb. Doublet of домкра́т (domkrát).
Borrowed from Dutch zonnedek (“cover from sun”).

parole.significato: sou'wester, southwester, cape ann (waterproof hat worn by sailors)
parole.testo: зюйд-ве́ст (zjujd-vést) + -ка (-ka), a calque of Dutch zuidwester or English sou'wester. The term derives from the observation that in the North Sea region, southwesterly wind often brings heavy rain.

parole.significato: cable (heavy rope or chain as used for mooring)
a type of a peaked cap with high cap band; fiddler cap, kashket
parole.testo: According to Shansky, from earlier forms карпуз (karpuz), карпуц (karpuc), from Dutch karpoets (“traveling hat”), and distinct from Etymology 2 (see below). The term originally referred to military cloth or fur hats; the “peaked cap” sense developed in mid-19th century.
Borrowed from Dutch kwitantie, see there for more. Compare Italian quietanza.
Borrowed from Dutch kiel or Low German Kiel.

parole.significato: wake (path left behind a ship on the surface of the water)
enema (injection of fluid into the rectum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch klysma or German Klysma.

Borrowed from Dutch kooi or Middle Low German kōje, ultimately from Latin cavea. In sense of a normal bed when used in informal speech compare Swedish krypa till kojs and Norwegian Nynorsk krypa til køys.
From Dutch komfoor, from Picard cauffoir equal to French chauffoir, from Latin calefacere.

Attested early 18th century in correspondence regarding Russia's purchase of weapons from Western Europe. The etymology is uncertain; there are several hypotheses. * Borrowed from Dutch korte sabel (“short saber”) + -ик (-ik, diminutive suffix). * From the obsolete term ко́рда (kórda, “short sword”)

parole.significato: korfball (team ballgame in which one scores by throwing the ball into a basket)
cruiser (naval vessel detached from the fleet)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch krengen (“to careen”, verb), from Middle Dutch crengen, causative of cringen. See also кренгова́ть (krengovátʹ).

parole.significato: to tack (to turn the bow through the wind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch laveren or German lavieren + -овать (-ovatʹ).
Borrowed from Dutch laag (“row of guns along one side of a ship”).

parole.significato: jackstay (taut wire, both ends of which are fixed to the ship structures)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch leier, from leiden (“to lead”).
Borrowed from Dutch lijf (“corsage”). Doublet of лейб- (lejb-).

parole.significato: lottery (scheme for the distribution of prizes by lot or chance)
pilot (specialist who navigates ships in dangerous areas, ports, etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch loodsman. Compare English lodesman.

parole.significato: top (on sailing vessels, a platform around the head of a lower mast)
sailor, seaman (a common member of the crew of a vessel; an enlisted man in the Navy)

parole.testo: From older ма́шта (mášta), from Dutch mast or Low German mast. Compare Polish maszt/maszta. For the change -шт- (-št-) → -чт- (-čt-) compare по́чта (póčta).
Borrowed from Dutch passaat. Omitting several steps, from Latin passus (whence also па (pa), пасса́ж (passáž), English pace, among others).

parole.significato: pitch (dark, extremely viscous material made by distilling tar)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch pek. Omitting several steps, from Latin pix.

Likely borrowed from Dutch papegaai. Attested since 1589. The sense of a unit of length originates from the Soviet animated cartoon «Тридцать восемь попугаев» («Tridcatʹ vosemʹ popugajev») (1976), where animals measured the length of a boa constrictor by comparing him to a parrot.

parole.significato: spar (linear object used as a mast, sprit, yard, boom, pole or gaff)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch rondhout, first recorded as ронго́ут (rongóut).

parole.significato: yard, a crossways-mast on a ship
flight (a specific journey made by an aircraft)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch roer, via an intermediate form *рурь (*rurʹ).
Borrowed from Dutch roeper, from roepen (“to shout”).

parole.significato: stopper (device for holding parts in place)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch stopper. First attested in Russian in the form "стоперс" in 1720.

parole.significato: chain hoist, chain block, pulley block, hoisting tackle, block and tackle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch talie, from Italian taglia.
Borrowed from Dutch tijk or English tick.
Borrowed from Dutch top, English top, or Low German Topp.
Borrowed from Dutch 't ruim (from het ruim). Omitting several steps, from Proto-Germanic *rūmą (whence also English room).
Derived from Dutch oester + -ица (-ica). First recorded in 1724. Cognate with Ukrainian у́стриця (ústrycja) and Belarusian ву́стрыца (vústryca).
Borrowed from Dutch vlag. Influenced by English flag (as by spelling with ⟨ф⟩ instead of ⟨в⟩) so as not to clash with влах (vlax, “Vlach”). The programming sense is a semantic loan from English flag.
Borrowed from Dutch vlaggestok (“flagpole”), from vlag (“flag”) + stok (“pole”). Influenced by English flag (as by spelling with ф instead of в) so as not to clash with влах (vlax, “Vlach”).

parole.significato: wooden or steel beam in the bow of the ship

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch zwabber or dialectal German Schwabber.

parole.significato: guy, guy line, sheet rope (support cable)
lock, sluice (of a canal or dam)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch sluis or German Schleuse. Further from Latin exclūsus, p.p.p. of exclūdō. Piecewise doublet with исключи́ть (isključítʹ).
Borrowed from Dutch sloep, from Middle French chaloupe, chaloppe, from Old French eschalope, escalope (via PIE related to Old Church Slavonic сколика (skolika, “shell”), English shell).

parole.significato: corkscrew (implement for opening bottles sealed by a cork)

parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch storm or Middle Low German storm. Doublet of штурм (šturm), borrowed from German.

parole.significato: helm, steering wheel (of a ship or an airplane)
cabin boy, ship's boy (a boy serving on a ship)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Dutch jongen. Compare German Junge.
